clinicalPearls: Disorder of remnant lipoprotein clearance caused by dysfunctional apolipoprotein E, classically homozygosity for the apoE2 isoform, though the phenotype requires a second metabolic hit to become manifest.
Characterised by a mixed hyperlipidaemia in which total cholesterol and triglycerides are elevated roughly in parallel, reflecting accumulation of cholesterol-enriched remnant particles.
Palmar crease xanthomata (xanthomata striata palmaris) are close to pathognomonic, and tuberoeruptive xanthomata over elbows and knees are characteristic.
Confers a markedly increased risk of premature coronary and, notably, peripheral arterial disease.
Most apoE2 homozygotes never develop the disease; expression typically needs a superimposed factor such as obesity, diabetes, hypothyroidism, oestrogen change or ageing.
The apoE2/E2 recessive form is commonest, but rarer dominant apoE variants can produce the phenotype in heterozygotes with earlier onset.
Responds well to treatment: weight loss, control of secondary factors, fibrates and statins can dramatically improve the lipid profile and regress xanthomata.
A raised ratio of VLDL cholesterol to plasma triglyceride, or detection of cholesterol-rich beta-migrating VLDL, supports the diagnosis.
reference.pathophysiology: Familial dysbetalipoproteinaemia is a disorder of hepatic clearance of triglyceride-rich lipoprotein remnants. Apolipoprotein E is the principal ligand by which chylomicron remnants and intermediate-density lipoproteins are recognised and taken up by the hepatic LDL receptor and LDL-receptor-related protein. The common apoE2 isoform binds these receptors poorly, so in apoE2 homozygotes remnant particles are cleared inefficiently and accumulate in plasma. Because this defect impairs remnant catabolism rather than triglyceride lipolysis, the retained particles are partially delipidated, cholesterol-enriched remnants that migrate in the beta position on electrophoresis, producing the classic broad beta band and a mixed elevation of cholesterol and triglyceride that rise together. Crucially, defective apoE binding alone is usually insufficient: most apoE2 homozygotes have normal or even low lipids, and the full phenotype emerges only when a second factor increases remnant production or further impairs receptor-mediated clearance, such as insulin resistance, obesity, type 2 diabetes, hypothyroidism, oestrogen withdrawal at menopause or renal disease. The cholesterol-laden remnants are highly atherogenic, readily taken up by arterial macrophages to form foam cells, which explains the strong predisposition to both coronary and peripheral vascular disease, while remnant deposition in skin and tendon produces the distinctive palmar and tuberoeruptive xanthomata.
additionalDifferentials: Familial combined hyperlipidaemia with overproduction of apoB-containing particles
Familial hypercholesterolaemia (isolated LDL elevation without proportional triglyceride rise)
Familial hypertriglyceridaemia and familial chylomicronaemia syndrome
Secondary mixed hyperlipidaemia from uncontrolled diabetes, hypothyroidism or nephrotic syndrome
Polygenic (common) mixed dyslipidaemia of the metabolic syndrome
Cholestatic liver disease with lipoprotein-X accumulation
Sitosterolaemia in the context of xanthomata with a family history
additionalInvestigations: Fasting lipid profile demonstrating parallel elevation of cholesterol and triglycerides
ApoE genotyping or phenotyping to confirm E2/E2 status or a rare dominant apoE variant
Calculation of the VLDL-cholesterol to total triglyceride ratio and apoB measurement (relatively low apoB for the lipid burden)
Lipoprotein electrophoresis or ultracentrifugation seeking beta-migrating VLDL (broad beta pattern)
Screening for secondary precipitants with glucose/HbA1c, thyroid function and renal profile
Cardiovascular risk assessment including peripheral arterial evaluation
Liver function tests before and during lipid-lowering therapy
redFlags: Symptoms of premature coronary disease such as exertional chest pain in a young or middle-aged patient
Claudication or critical limb ischaemia indicating advanced peripheral arterial disease
Rapidly progressive or extensive xanthomata suggesting poor metabolic control
Very high combined lipids with abdominal pain, raising concern for coexistent severe hypertriglyceridaemia and pancreatitis
New decompensation of lipids coinciding with hypothyroidism or uncontrolled diabetes
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is favourable when the diagnosis is made and the condition treated, as the dyslipidaemia and xanthomata usually respond strikingly to lifestyle measures and lipid-lowering therapy. Untreated, the marked atherogenic remnant burden drives premature coronary and peripheral vascular disease and its associated morbidity and mortality.
pitfalls: Missing the diagnosis because apoE2 homozygosity is common yet only a minority express disease, so genotype alone neither confirms nor excludes it.
Mislabelling the mixed lipid pattern as ordinary combined hyperlipidaemia and overlooking the distinctive remnant biochemistry and palmar xanthomata.
Using standard LDL-cholesterol equations, which are unreliable when remnant particles dominate the profile.
Failing to seek and treat the secondary precipitant that unmasked the disorder, limiting response to therapy.
Underestimating peripheral arterial risk by focusing only on coronary assessment.
references: Standard clinical lipidology and metabolic medicine textbooks
